architectureNotes:
Three-layer, LLM-agnostic by design.

Layer 1 (ingest): tree-sitter parses the repo; parser.py plus ~9 language/framework resolvers extract symbols and relationships. incremental.py + the watchdog daemon keep it current.

Layer 2 (store/query): a local SQLite database with versioned migrations and an FTS index, wrapped by graph.py and networkx for traversal, communities.py for clustering, flows.py for execution paths, changes.py for diff-to-symbol mapping, embeddings.py for semantic search.

Layer 3 (serve): the same data is exposed four ways — an MCP server (main.py + tools/*, fastmcp), a CLI (`code-review-graph`, cli.py at 76 KB), a GitHub Action (action.yml + render_pr_comment.py), and a VS Code extension that bypasses Python entirely and reads the SQLite file from TypeScript.

The crucial design property for aio-ade: the tool is a *context provider*, not a reviewer. It performs no LLM inference for review. The judgement lives in the connected agent, steered by the five prompt workflows in prompts.py and the seven skills in skills/. The whole system is an argument that the bottleneck in AI code review is context selection, not model quality — hence detail_level tiering, the "call get_minimal_context first" rule, the 3-tool-calls-per-turn cap, and an entire eval suite measuring token efficiency.

Its notion of severity is structural rather than semantic: a float risk score with bands at ~0.4 and ~0.7, a test_gap_count, and flow criticality scores. It does not classify findings as security/perf/style — that is left to the agent. If aio-ade wants a finding taxonomy (which its reportFindings-style UI implies), it must supply one; the two layers compose cleanly, with the graph deciding *where to look* and Claude/Codex deciding *what is wrong*.

features.howItWorks: pyproject.toml dependency list contains only mcp, fastmcp, tree-sitter, tree-sitter-language-pack, pyyaml, networkx, watchdog, tomli. The only LLM-adjacent optional extras are sentence-transformers (local embeddings), google-generativeai (embeddings only), and ollama (used by wiki.py for doc generation). The reviewing intelligence is entirely delegated to whatever agent is connected over MCP — i.e. Claude Code or Codex itself. code_review_graph/main.py (43 KB) is the MCP server; code_review_graph/tools/*.py are the MCP tool implementations.
features.name: CORRECTION: this is not a LangGraph multi-agent review pipeline
features.valueForAioIde: Changes the integration calculus completely. There is no agent graph to port, so option (b) from the brief ("reimplement the review graph in TS and run each node via claude -p") has almost nothing to reimplement on the agent side, while the part that *is* substantial (a 626 KB multi-language tree-sitter parser) is the part you least want to rewrite. The correct move is to let aio-ade's claude/codex CLIs talk to it as an MCP server and to consume its SQLite output from TypeScript for UI.
features.whatItDoes: The research brief assumed a LangGraph state machine of review steps. It is not. There is no langgraph/langchain dependency, no node/edge/conditional-routing state machine, no State TypedDict, and no direct Anthropic/OpenAI SDK call anywhere in the declared dependencies. The "graph" in the name is a *code* knowledge graph (symbols and their call/import/test relationships), not an agent workflow graph.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/main.py registers tools defined across code_review_graph/tools/{build,query,review,context,analysis_tools,community_tools,docs,flows_tools,refactor_tools,registry_tools}.py via fastmcp. Tool names confirmed from prompts.py: get_minimal_context, detect_changes, query_graph(pattern="callers_of"|"tests_for", target=...), get_affected_flows, get_review_context, get_impact_radius, get_architecture_overview, list_flows, get_flow, list_communities, get_community, semantic_search_nodes, list_graph_stats, refactor(mode="dead_code"), find_large_functions. Server entry is also reachable as `python -m code_review_graph` (__main__.py) and there is a .mcp.json in the repo root wiring it for Claude Code.
features.name: MCP server with detail_level token tiering
features.valueForAioIde: Both target agents speak MCP. Registering this one server gives Claude Code and Codex identical structural review context with zero per-agent adapter code — exactly the parity aio-ade needs when the same task can be dispatched to either CLI.
features.whatItDoes: Exposes ~20 graph query tools over MCP (stdio), every one accepting detail_level="minimal" | "standard" | "verbose" so an agent can pay only for the resolution it needs.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/changes.py (19 KB) plus code_review_graph/tools/review.py (17 KB). The risk contract is visible verbatim in prompts.py routing logic: `If risk is "low"` vs `"medium" or "high"`, `If risk > 0.4`, `if risk > 0.7`, and `If test_gap_count > 0`. So risk is a float in roughly 0..1 with banded thresholds at ~0.4 and ~0.7, and test gaps are counted separately. tests/fixtures/detect_changes_sample.json (3990 bytes) is the golden output shape. NOTE: I did not read changes.py or review.py, so the exact field names and weighting formula are inferred from the prompt text and the fixture filename, not confirmed.
features.name: detect_changes: git-diff-aware change analysis with a numeric risk score
features.valueForAioIde: This is the single most valuable primitive for the planned inline diff review panel: it is already diff-shaped, already keyed to files/symbols, and already carries a severity-like score you can sort and color by. It also gives you a pre-agent triage gate so you only burn Claude/Codex tokens on medium/high-risk diffs.
features.whatItDoes: Takes the working-tree/branch diff, maps changed hunks to graph symbols, and returns a change list plus a risk score, a low/medium/high risk band, and a test_gap_count.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/graph.py (86 KB) holds the traversal; networkx does the reachability. The VS Code extension surfaces it as code-review-graph-vscode/src/features/blastRadius.ts (2996 bytes) — a small, readable TS consumer of the same data.
features.name: Blast radius / impact radius (get_impact_radius, query_graph callers_of)
features.valueForAioIde: aio-ade runs agents in parallel git worktrees. Blast radius across worktrees answers the question the product actually has: "do these two agents' diffs collide semantically, not just textually?" Two agents editing different files can still break each other through a shared callee, and line-level git merge detection cannot see that.
features.whatItDoes: Given a changed symbol, walks the call graph to enumerate everything transitively affected, and inversely finds tests that cover a symbol (pattern="tests_for").

features.howItWorks: code-review-graph-vscode/src/backend/sqlite.ts (17755 bytes) is the schema-aware query layer; backend/cli.ts (6420 bytes) shells out to the Python CLI for builds; backend/watcher.ts (1914 bytes) watches for DB changes. UI: views/graphWebview.ts (20219 B), webview/graph.ts (30640 B), views/treeView.ts + treeItems.ts + statusBar.ts. Features: features/scmDecorations.ts (4988 B), features/reviewAssistant.ts (3599 B), features/navigation.ts (7264 B), features/search.ts, features/cursorResolver.ts. Built with esbuild.mjs. There is even test/sqlite.test.ts (17507 B) covering the reader. NOTE: I enumerated these files and their sizes but did not read their contents.
features.name: TypeScript SQLite reader + VS Code extension (the real gift)
features.valueForAioIde: This removes most of the TypeScript work. sqlite.ts is a drop-in replacement for writing your own reader, scmDecorations.ts is a direct blueprint for annotating Orca's existing source-control/diff UI, and reviewAssistant.ts shows the intended agent-facing flow. Its VS Code API surface (TreeDataProvider, webview, SCM decorations) maps onto React components with mechanical effort, and vitest can absorb sqlite.test.ts.
features.whatItDoes: A complete, MIT-licensed TypeScript client that reads the graph SQLite database directly and renders navigation, search, SCM decorations, a blast-radius view, a review assistant and an interactive graph webview.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/prompts.py (6491 bytes), read in full. The shared preamble is: (1) ALWAYS call get_minimal_context first with a task description; (2) use detail_level="minimal" on all tool calls unless insufficient; (3) only escalate to "standard"/"verbose" for specific entities needing deeper inspection; (4) never request more than 3 tool calls per turn unless absolutely necessary; (5) prefer targeted queries (query_graph with a specific symbol) over broad scans (list_communities with full members); (6) when reviewing changes: detect_changes(detail_level="minimal") then only expand on high-risk items. review_changes(base="HEAD~1") then routes on risk band and ends with "Do NOT call get_review_context unless you need source code snippets for a specific function." pre_merge_check(base="HEAD~1") escalates at risk>0.4 and risk>0.7, checks tests_for on up to 3 untested functions, runs refactor(mode="dead_code") for newly dead code, and demands the output "GO/NO-GO recommendation with 1-sentence justification + list of required follow-ups." Returned as fastmcp Message(role="user", ...) objects; a _user() helper notes fastmcp >=3.2 rejects raw dicts.
features.name: Five MCP prompt workflows (fully extracted, verbatim)
features.valueForAioIde: These are the reusable prompt asset the brief asked for, and they transfer even if you integrate nothing else. Port them as aio-ade review presets ("Review changes", "Pre-merge GO/NO-GO", "Explain architecture", "Onboard", "Debug") issued to claude -p / codex exec. The GO/NO-GO + required-follow-ups output contract is a much better fit for a desktop review panel than free-form prose.
features.whatItDoes: Ships review_changes, architecture_map, debug_issue, onboard_developer and pre_merge_check as MCP prompts. Each is a numbered tool-call plan with explicit escalation rules, prefixed by a shared token-efficiency preamble.

features.howItWorks: skills/{build-graph,debug-issue,explore-codebase,refactor-safely,review-changes,review-delta,review-pr}/SKILL.md. review-pr/SKILL.md (2405 B) and review-delta/SKILL.md (2180 B) are the largest, so they carry the most checklist detail. Installation/uninstallation is automated by code_review_graph/skills.py (71 KB) and code_review_graph/uninstall.py (42 KB) — that much code implies it writes into ~/.claude/skills, .mcp.json, hooks and settings across several host tools. hooks/hooks.json + hooks/session-start.sh install a Claude Code session-start hook. NOTE: I did not read the SKILL.md bodies; their exact checklists are unverified.
features.name: Claude Code Skills bundle (7 skills), including review-pr and review-delta
features.valueForAioIde: aio-ade already manages Claude Code configuration for its worktrees, so it can install these skills into each worktree's .claude directory instead of letting the Python installer mutate the user's global config. The review-pr and review-delta bodies are the second-highest-value prompt extraction after prompts.py and are worth fetching before implementation.
features.whatItDoes: Installs first-class Claude Code skills so the review workflows are invocable by name rather than pasted as prompts.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/flows.py (25 KB), surfaced as list_flows / get_flow / get_affected_flows. prompts.py confirms flows carry "criticality scores" and that get_affected_flows is the escalation step when a diff touches more than 3 changed functions. Benchmarked by eval/benchmarks/flow_completeness.py.
features.name: Flows: named critical execution paths with criticality scores
features.valueForAioIde: Turns "12 files changed" into "this touches the auth and checkout flows" — the sentence a reviewer actually wants at the top of a review panel, and a natural grouping header for inline findings.
features.whatItDoes: Derives end-to-end execution flows (e.g. HTTP route -> handler -> service -> DB) from the graph, scores each by criticality, and reports which flows a diff touches.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/incremental.py (61 KB) is the largest non-parser module; daemon.py (39 KB) + daemon_cli.py (9 KB) provide a separate `crg-daemon` console script; watchdog is a hard dependency; http_origin_guard.py (7 KB) suggests the daemon also exposes a local HTTP surface with origin checks. graph_diff.py (3.6 KB) diffs graph states. The VS Code extension mirrors this with backend/watcher.ts.
features.name: Incremental graph updates + file-watching daemon
features.valueForAioIde: Essential if the review panel is to feel live while agents are actively writing code in a worktree. Also a caution: one daemon per worktree times N parallel worktrees is real memory and file-handle pressure that aio-ade would have to supervise, and the local HTTP surface needs an auth/origin review before it is spawned on a user machine.
features.whatItDoes: Keeps the graph fresh after each edit without a full re-parse, via a background daemon watching the filesystem.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/parser.py is 625,985 bytes — by far the bulk of the project. tests/fixtures/ evidences coverage: C, C++, C#, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Scala, Swift, Ruby, PHP, Python, TS/TSX, Vue, Lua/Luau, Dart, Elixir, Julia, Nix, Perl/XS, R, ReScript, Solidity, SQL, SystemVerilog, Zig, GDScript, Objective-C, shell, Ansible YAML, Terraform HCL, dbt, Databricks notebooks, Jupyter. Language-specific resolvers are separate modules: jedi_resolver.py, python_resolver.py, tsconfig_resolver.py, spring_resolver.py, hcl_resolver.py, rescript_resolver.py, temporal_resolver.py, scoped_resolver.py, event_resolver.py. custom_languages.py (12.7 KB) allows user-defined grammars.
features.name: Multi-language tree-sitter parser covering ~25+ languages
features.valueForAioIde: This is the moat and the reason not to reimplement in TypeScript. It is also the strongest argument for tolerating a Python dependency: you get 25+ languages for free versus writing your own tree-sitter layer per language.
features.whatItDoes: Parses source into symbols and relationships across a very wide language set, including framework-aware resolution.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/communities.py (37 KB), optional igraph extra, exposed as list_communities / get_community / get_architecture_overview. The architecture_map prompt instructs the agent to "Produce a concise Mermaid diagram showing communities as boxes and key flows as arrows."
features.name: Community detection / architecture overview
features.valueForAioIde: Useful for the onboarding/orientation surface and for auto-labelling which subsystem an agent's worktree is touching. Lower priority than the diff-review path.
features.whatItDoes: Clusters the graph into modules ("communities"), scores inter-community coupling, and produces a 30-second architectural mental model plus a Mermaid diagram.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/embeddings.py (45,954 B) and search.py (16 KB); tests/test_fts_sync.py confirms an FTS index kept in sync. Embeddings are optional extras: sentence-transformers (fully local) or google-generativeai (API). Benchmarked by eval/benchmarks/search_quality.py and multi_hop_retrieval.py.
features.name: Semantic search over symbols and docstrings
features.valueForAioIde: Nice, but aio-ade's agents already have their own search tools. The differentiator here is local-only embeddings with no API egress, which matters if the app markets privacy. Not on the critical path.
features.whatItDoes: Embedding-backed search (semantic_search_nodes) plus SQLite FTS keyword search.

features.howItWorks: action.yml (5126 B, composite action), .github/workflows/pr-review.yml (1311 B, the simple path) and pr-review-comment.yml (7003 B, the commenting path), with scripts/render_pr_comment.py (13,054 B) doing the markdown rendering. Contract-tested by tests/test_action_render.py (12,855 B) and tests/test_pr_review_workflows.py. Documented in docs/GITHUB_ACTION.md (8584 B). NOTE: I did not read render_pr_comment.py; the exact markdown section layout and any severity emoji/label taxonomy live there and should be read before building the UI.
features.name: GitHub Action + PR comment renderer (concrete output format)
features.valueForAioIde: render_pr_comment.py is effectively a reference implementation of "turn graph review output into a human-readable review document," and its test file pins the expected format. Port it to a React renderer for the inline diff panel rather than inventing a layout. This is the highest-value file I did not get to read.
features.whatItDoes: Runs the review in CI and posts a rendered markdown review comment on the PR.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/context_savings.py (11 KB), token_benchmark.py, and an eval package: eval/runner.py (13 KB), eval/reporter.py (10 KB), eval/scorer.py (2.6 KB), benchmarks for token_efficiency, impact_accuracy, multi_hop_retrieval, search_quality, flow_completeness, build_performance and agent_baseline. Configs per target repo (express, fastapi, flask, gin, httpx, itself) in eval/configs/*.yaml, with committed CSV results under evaluate/results/ dated 2026-05-25. Driven in CI by .github/workflows/eval.yml. docs/REPRODUCING.md (21 KB) documents reproduction.
features.name: Context savings measurement + token efficiency eval harness
features.valueForAioIde: Two uses. First, the methodology is a template for proving aio-ade's own agent-orchestration efficiency claims. Second, a live "tokens saved on this review" figure is a cheap, honest UI element for a product whose users pay per token.
features.whatItDoes: Quantifies how many tokens the graph saves versus naive file-dumping, with a repeatable benchmark suite and published results.

features.howItWorks: docs/schema.md (276 lines) plus code_review_graph/migrations.py (9970 B) and tests/test_migrations.py. The VS Code extension's backend/sqlite.ts queries this schema directly rather than going through the Python CLI. NOTE: I listed docs/schema.md but did not read it.
features.name: Documented SQLite schema
features.valueForAioIde: This is what makes the hybrid integration safe: the Python side owns writing the DB, and aio-ade's main process can read it directly with better-sqlite3 for fast UI queries — no IPC round-trip per hover, no Python in the render path. Read docs/schema.md and sqlite.ts together before designing the data layer, and pin a schema version since migrations.py implies it moves.
features.whatItDoes: Publishes the on-disk graph schema, with versioned migrations.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/refactor.py (36 KB) and tools/refactor_tools.py; invoked in the pre_merge_check prompt as refactor(mode="dead_code", detail_level="minimal") to catch "newly dead code" introduced by a diff. analysis.py (13 KB) + tools/analysis_tools.py back find_large_functions. There are dedicated dead-guard fixtures for C, Go and TS.
features.name: refactor and dead-code analysis
features.valueForAioIde: "Your change orphaned this function" is a finding class agents routinely miss and that aio-ade can surface deterministically, without an LLM call. Cheap, high-signal addition to the review panel.
features.whatItDoes: Graph-driven refactor assistance including dead code detection, plus find_large_functions.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/visualization.py is 99,350 bytes and is ruff-exempted for E501 with the comment "embedded HTML/JS template" — i.e. it is a large HTML/JS bundle inlined in Python. The VS Code extension reimplements this properly in TypeScript: views/graphWebview.ts (20 KB) + webview/graph.ts (30 KB). exports.py (14 KB) handles other export formats.
features.name: Graph visualization webview
features.valueForAioIde: Take the TypeScript version, not the Python one. aio-ade is already an Electron renderer, so webview/graph.ts is closer to a React component than a Python-templated HTML blob is. Treat this as a later polish feature, well behind the diff review panel.
features.whatItDoes: Interactive HTML/JS graph visualization of the codebase.

features.howItWorks: code_review_graph/wiki.py (10,610 B) with the optional `wiki` extra pulling ollama>=0.1.0. This is the only place the project itself drives an LLM for content generation.
features.name: Wiki generation via Ollama
features.valueForAioIde: Redundant. aio-ade already has two far stronger models on tap; if you want generated docs, prompt Claude or Codex with the graph context instead of adding an Ollama dependency. Skip.
features.whatItDoes: Generates repository documentation from the graph using a local LLM.

features.howItWorks: memory.py (3.8 KB), hints.py (12 KB), forget.py (7 KB) with test_forget_parity.py, registry.py (10 KB) + tools/registry_tools.py, postprocessing.py (6.4 KB), enrich.py (9.4 KB), constants.py, config_keys.py.
features.name: Memory, hints, forget, registry, postprocessing subsystems
features.valueForAioIde: Internal plumbing; nothing to lift directly. forget.py is worth a glance if aio-ade needs to invalidate graph state when a worktree is destroyed, which it will.
features.whatItDoes: Auxiliary state: persistent memory, heuristic hints, selective forgetting of stale graph state, a symbol registry, and post-parse cleanup.

features.howItWorks: tests/test_windows_compat.py (3448 B) plus a CI matrix in .github/workflows/ci.yml (3790 B). NOTE: I did not read ci.yml, so I cannot confirm the OS matrix actually includes windows-latest.
features.name: Windows compatibility is explicitly tested
features.valueForAioIde: Directly relevant: the primary aio-ade development environment is Windows 11, and subprocess/path handling is where cross-platform Python integrations usually break. Worth verifying against the CI matrix before committing to the subprocess approach.
features.whatItDoes: Carries a dedicated Windows compatibility test module.

integrationRisks: Python runtime dependency is unavoidable if you want the parser. parser.py alone is 626 KB covering 25+ languages; reimplementing it in TypeScript is not a realistic scope. Bundling CPython plus tree-sitter native wheels into an Electron installer adds serious weight and per-platform build complexity. Mitigate by detecting `uv`/`uvx`/`pipx` and offering guided install (`uvx code-review-graph`) rather than bundling — the VS Code extension already does exactly this in src/onboarding/installer.ts, so there is a reference implementation.

Native module and ABI friction on Windows 11 (the primary dev environment). tree-sitter-language-pack ships prebuilt wheels but sentence-transformers, igraph and numpy extras are heavier; keep optional extras out of the default install path. tests/test_windows_compat.py exists but I did not verify the CI OS matrix.

Aggressive global config mutation. skills.py is 71 KB and uninstall.py is 42 KB — that volume strongly implies the installer writes into user-global locations (~/.claude, .mcp.json, hooks, editor settings) across multiple host tools. aio-ade must not let it rewrite a user's global Claude Code config; scope all installs to the worktree or to aio-ade's own managed config directory, and audit skills.py before shipping.

Daemon fan-out. One watchdog daemon per worktree, multiplied by N parallel worktrees, means N Python processes plus N file watchers plus N SQLite files. Needs lifecycle supervision tied to worktree create/destroy (see forget.py) or it will leak processes.

Local HTTP surface. http_origin_guard.py (7.4 KB) implies daemon.py exposes HTTP with origin checking. Any locally bound port spawned on a user's machine needs an explicit auth/binding review before release — confirm it binds loopback only and requires a token. Unverified.

Graph build cost and staleness on first run. A cold full-repo parse on a large monorepo is not instant; the review panel needs an honest indexing state rather than an empty panel, and stale-graph results must be visibly marked.

Schema drift. Reading SQLite directly from TypeScript couples aio-ade to an internal schema that migrations.py actively versions. Pin a supported version range and fail loudly with a clear message on mismatch instead of returning wrong data.

Unverified specifics in this report. I read LICENSE, pyproject.toml and prompts.py in full and enumerated the complete file tree with sizes. I did NOT read README.md (41 KB), action.yml, render_pr_comment.py, changes.py, tools/review.py, docs/schema.md, docs/architecture.md, or any VS Code extension source. Claims about exact risk-score field names, the PR-comment markdown layout, and the SKILL.md checklist contents are inferred from prompt text, filenames and file sizes — confirm before implementing types or UI.

Dependency currency. fastmcp is pinned >=3.2.4,<4 with an inline comment citing CVE-2025-62800/62801/66416 and a note that fastmcp 3.0 broke the server. The MCP ecosystem is moving fast; expect churn and pin deliberately.

Single-maintainer project. One author, version 2.3.7, "Development Status :: 4 - Beta". Bus-factor risk on a dependency sitting in your review path. Partly mitigated by MIT licensing and a very large test suite (tests/ totals well over 1 MB, e.g. test_parser.py 101 KB, test_multilang.py 157 KB, test_tools.py 93 KB), so a fork is maintainable if needed.
license: MIT, verified by reading LICENSE at repo root: "MIT License / Copyright (c) 2026 Tirth Kanani". pyproject.toml also declares license = "MIT". Fully compatible with vendoring into an MIT Electron app, provided the copyright notice is retained in the vendored files. The TypeScript VS Code extension carries its own identical MIT LICENSE (code-review-graph-vscode/LICENSE), so its sources are the cleanest thing to vendor.
oneLiner: A local-first code knowledge graph (tree-sitter parse -> SQLite + networkx) exposed to AI coding agents over MCP, CLI, a GitHub Action and a VS Code extension, so agents can review diffs with blast-radius/risk context instead of dumping the whole repo into the prompt.
project: code-review-graph (PyPI: code-review-graph, v2.3.7, by Tirth Kanani / tirth8205)
reusablePointers: code_review_graph/prompts.py (6.5 KB) — READ IN FULL. The five prompt workflows and the six-rule token-efficiency preamble, verbatim. Highest reuse-to-effort ratio in the repo; port straight to aio-ade review presets. The pre_merge_check GO/NO-GO output contract is the best UI-ready format here.

code-review-graph-vscode/src/backend/sqlite.ts (17.8 KB) — MIT TypeScript reader for the graph SQLite schema. Vendor this instead of writing your own; pair with test/sqlite.test.ts (17.5 KB) which ports to vitest almost unchanged.

code-review-graph-vscode/src/features/scmDecorations.ts (5.0 KB) — annotates the VS Code source-control view with graph data. This is the closest existing analogue to the inline diff review panel Orca needs.
code-review-graph-vscode/src/features/blastRadius.ts (3.0 KB) — compact TS consumer of impact analysis; the semantic-collision check for parallel worktrees.
code-review-graph-vscode/src/features/reviewAssistant.ts (3.6 KB) — the extension's own agent-facing review flow; shows how they intended graph + LLM to compose in an editor.

scripts/render_pr_comment.py (13.1 KB) + tests/test_action_render.py (12.9 KB) — the review-output markdown format and its pinned expectations. THE most important file I did not read; read it before designing the review panel layout.
skills/review-pr/SKILL.md (2.4 KB) and skills/review-delta/SKILL.md (2.2 KB) — the remaining prompt/checklist assets, unread. Fetch alongside review-changes/SKILL.md.
docs/schema.md (276 lines) + code_review_graph/migrations.py — the SQLite contract underpinning direct TS reads. Pin a schema version.

code_review_graph/changes.py (19 KB) + code_review_graph/tools/review.py (17 KB) + tests/fixtures/detect_changes_sample.json — the risk-scoring implementation and its golden output shape. Unread; read to confirm exact field names before building types.
code_review_graph/context_savings.py (11 KB) + code_review_graph/eval/ — methodology for proving token savings; template for aio-ade's own efficiency metrics.

docs/architecture.md (120 lines), docs/LLM-OPTIMIZED-REFERENCE.md (4.7 KB), docs/GITHUB_ACTION.md, docs/COMMANDS.md (13.4 KB), docs/FEATURES.md (15.3 KB) — orientation docs; LLM-OPTIMIZED-REFERENCE.md is deliberately compact and force-included into the wheel.
.mcp.json (128 B) + hooks/hooks.json + hooks/session-start.sh — the exact Claude Code wiring, copyable per-worktree.
stack: Python >=3.10 (hatchling build, ~2.2 MB of source in code_review_graph/). Core deps: mcp>=1.0, fastmcp>=3.2.4,<4, tree-sitter>=0.23 + tree-sitter-language-pack, networkx>=3.2, pyyaml, watchdog (file-watch daemon), tomli (py<3.11). Storage is SQLite (own migrations.py + FTS). Optional extras: sentence-transformers+numpy (local embeddings), google-generativeai (embedding API), igraph (community detection), ollama (wiki generation), jedi (Python enrichment), matplotlib (eval charts). Dev: pytest/pytest-asyncio/ruff/mypy. Also ships a separate TypeScript VS Code extension (code-review-graph-vscode/, esbuild, reads the SQLite DB directly) and a composite GitHub Action (action.yml + scripts/render_pr_comment.py).
verdict:
Hybrid: register as an MCP server (subprocess) + vendor the TypeScript layer. Not a straight reimplementation, and definitely not inspiration-only.

First, correct the premise: there is no LangGraph review graph to port. This is a tree-sitter code knowledge graph that feeds context to whatever agent is attached. That reframes the brief's three options.

Option (a) spawn Python — recommended, with a caveat. Do not bundle CPython. Detect `uv`/`uvx`/`pipx` and offer guided install, exactly as the project's own VS Code extension does in src/onboarding/installer.ts. Then register the MCP server for both `claude` and `codex`, which both speak MCP, so you get agent parity for free with no per-CLI adapter. Cost: a real external dependency and a graceful-degradation path when Python is absent. Benefit: 25+ languages of parsing you did not write.

Option (b) reimplement in TypeScript — reject as specified, adopt in part. There is no agent graph worth reimplementing, and the part that matters (626 KB of parser plus nine resolvers) is XL-to-unrealistic. But the TypeScript client layer already exists under MIT in code-review-graph-vscode/, so vendor sqlite.ts, blastRadius.ts and scmDecorations.ts to power the inline diff review panel with direct better-sqlite3 reads from Electron's main process. No Python in the render path, no IPC per hover.

Option (c) inspiration-only — insufficient alone, but take it immediately and unconditionally. prompts.py is free value available today: the six-rule token-efficiency preamble, the five workflows, the risk bands at 0.4/0.7, and the "GO/NO-GO + 1-sentence justification + required follow-ups" output contract. Ship these as aio-ade review presets before any Python integration lands.

Suggested sequencing. Phase 1 (S, no dependency): port the five prompt workflows as review presets for `claude -p` and `codex exec`, and define your own finding severity taxonomy since the tool deliberately does not supply one. Phase 2 (M): optional MCP integration behind a feature flag, with detection and guided install, scoped strictly to aio-ade's managed config so nothing touches the user's global Claude Code setup. Phase 3 (L): vendor sqlite.ts and build the inline diff review panel on direct SQLite reads, using scmDecorations.ts as the blueprint and render_pr_comment.py as the layout reference. Phase 4 (nice-to-have): cross-worktree blast-radius collision detection — the genuinely novel capability for a parallel-agent IDE, since git detects textual conflicts but not semantic ones.

Before implementing, read the five files I could not reach: scripts/render_pr_comment.py, code_review_graph/changes.py, code_review_graph/tools/review.py, docs/schema.md, and skills/review-pr/SKILL.md. Those pin the output format, the risk-score field names, and the remaining checklists.
